issues.legal_issue: A transfer made for consideration does not satisfy the statutory definition of a gift.
material_facts: The appellant executed a document styled as a gift deed, and it was admitted that the transfer was made for consideration, part of which had been paid and the balance promised.
issues.conclusion: The deed was not a completed gift because a gift must be made without consideration.
issues.legal_principle: Section 122 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 defines a gift as a voluntary transfer without consideration, accepted by or on behalf of the donee. The Court relied on Naramadaben Maganlal Thakker v. Pranivandas Maganlal Thakker, (1997) 2 SCC 255, which explains that execution of a registered gift deed, acceptance and delivery together complete a gift.

predicates.civil_appeal_about_a_purported_gift: The proceeding is a civil appeal concerning whether a document styled as a gift deed transferred property as a gift.
predicates.transfer_made_for_consideration: The purported transfer was made in exchange for consideration.
predicates.consideration_based_transfer_is_not_a_gi: A transfer made for consideration does not qualify as a gift.

issues.definition: When a civil appeal concerns a purported gift and the transfer was made for consideration, the transfer does not qualify as a gift.

issues.legal_issue: A purported gift conditioned to take effect only after the donor's death is not a completed gift during the donor's lifetime, and the donor may cancel it while it remains incomplete.
material_facts: The deed stated that the gift would take effect after the appellant and her husband's deaths.
The deed was also conditional on the respondent looking after the appellant and her husband.
The appellant cancelled the deed, and the Court found that no completed gift had been made.
issues.conclusion: There was no completed gift, and the appellant was entitled to cancel the deed.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 122 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, a gift is a transfer of existing property without consideration, accepted by or on behalf of the donee. Under Section 123, a gift of immovable property must be made by a registered, signed and attested instrument. A conditional gift becomes complete only when the conditions in the deed are complied with. The Court relied on Naramadaben Maganlal Thakker v. Pranivandas Maganlal Thakker, (1997) 2 SCC 255, concerning completion of a gift, and distinguished the valid gift in Reninkuntla Rajamma v. K. Sarwanamma, (2014) 9 SCC 445, where acceptance occurred during the donor's lifetime.

predicates.civil_appeal_about_a_purported_gift: The proceeding is a civil appeal concerning whether a document styled as a gift deed transferred property as a gift.
predicates.deed_conditioned_to_take_effect_after_do: The deed provides that the purported gift will take effect only after the donor's death.
predicates.donor_may_cancel_incomplete_gift: The donor may cancel a purported gift that did not become complete during the donor's lifetime.

issues.definition: If a civil appeal concerns a purported gift that is to take effect only after the donor's death, the donor may cancel it as an incomplete gift.

issues.legal_issue: A donor's retention of possession or enjoyment during the donor's lifetime does not, by itself, invalidate an otherwise completed gift.
material_facts: The Court considered the principle in a case involving a registered gift of immovable property that was accepted by the donee although the donor reserved possession and the right to receive rent during her lifetime.
The Court distinguished that situation from the deed before it, which was conditional and stated to take effect after the donor's death.
issues.conclusion: Retention of possession or enjoyment alone does not prevent a valid gift, provided the legal requirements for a gift are satisfied.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 122 and 123 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 require a gift to satisfy the statutory conditions for a gift and prescribe how a gift of immovable property is effected. Relying on Reninkuntla Rajamma v. K. Sarwanamma, (2014) 9 SCC 445, the Court held that ownership may be gifted without transferring possession, provided the gift is accepted during the donor's lifetime and the other requirements are met.
